title: Route 53 and CloudFront Quick Revision
summary: Night-before revision of Route 53 (hosted zones, records, alias, routing policies, health checks) and CloudFront (distributions, origins, cache behaviours, TTLs, invalidations, OAC for S3), from mental model to cheat sheet.

chapters.title: Route 53 and CloudFront at a Glance
points: Hosted zones and record types
Alias records
Routing policies
Health checks and failover
CloudFront distributions and origins
Cache behaviours, TTLs, invalidations
OAC for S3

chapters.title: Route 53 Mental Model: Zones and Records
points: Hosted zone = container of records for one domain; public zone answers internet queries, private zone answers only from associated VPCs; creating a zone gives 4 NS records, which must match the registrar's name servers
Record = name + type + value + TTL; A is IPv4, AAAA is IPv6, CNAME maps a name to another name, MX is mail, TXT is verification text, NS delegates a subdomain
CNAME vs Alias: CNAME is not allowed at the zone apex (example.com) and DNS queries to it are billed; Alias works at the apex, is free for AWS targets and returns A/AAAA directly
Alias targets: CloudFront, ALB/NLB, API Gateway, S3 website endpoint, Elastic Beanstalk, another record in the same zone; an alias cannot point to an EC2 DNS name
Example: example.com A alias to d111abcdef8.cloudfront.net, with a Route 53 alias, no TTL to set (inherits the target's)
Mistake: registrar NS not updated to the hosted zone's NS after recreating a zone, so DNS resolves nowhere

chapters.title: Routing Policies and Health Checks
points: Simple: one record, one or more values returned in random order; no health checks possible on it
Weighted: records share a name with weights 0-255; traffic share = weight / sum of weights; weight 0 stops traffic; used for canary and blue-green
Latency: answers with the region that has the lowest measured latency from the user to AWS regions; record is tagged with a region, not a measured distance to your server
Failover: active-passive with a primary and a secondary record; primary needs a health check; secondary is served when the primary is unhealthy
Geolocation routes by user's country or continent (compliance, localisation) and needs a Default record for unmatched locations; geoproximity needs Traffic Flow and uses bias

chapters.title: Health Checks and Everyday Route 53 Usage
points: Health check types: endpoint (HTTP, HTTPS, TCP; default interval 30s, fast 10s; unhealthy after 3 failures by default), calculated (combines other checks), CloudWatch alarm based (for private resources)
Health checkers are outside your VPC, so for a private endpoint use a CloudWatch alarm health check; allow the Route 53 health checker IP ranges in the security group for public ones
Create a record: aws route53 change-resource-record-sets --hosted-zone-id Z123 --change-batch file://change.json with Action UPSERT
Check an answer: dig example.com +short or aws route53 test-dns-answer --hosted-zone-id Z123 --record-name example.com --record-type A
Mistake: failover/weighted records with no health check attached, so a dead endpoint still gets traffic; also an alias record can use Evaluate Target Health instead of a separate check

chapters.title: CloudFront Distributions, Origins and Cache Behaviours
points: Distribution = a CDN config with a *.cloudfront.net domain; it serves from edge locations, a miss goes to a regional edge cache and then the origin
Origins: S3 bucket, ALB, API Gateway or any custom HTTP server; an origin group gives failover to a secondary origin on 5xx or 4xx errors

Cache behaviour matches a path pattern (/images/*, /api/*) and picks the origin, allowed methods, viewer protocol policy (redirect HTTP to HTTPS) and cache policy; patterns are evaluated in order, and Default (*) is last

Cache key = what makes two requests the same object (path plus any forwarded headers, cookies, query strings); forwarding more values means a lower hit ratio, so forward only what the origin needs; origin request policy forwards values without adding them to the key
Mistake: the ACM certificate for a custom domain must be in us-east-1, and the domain needs an alternate domain name (CNAME) set on the distribution

chapters.title: TTLs, Invalidations and OAC for S3
points: TTL: CloudFront honours origin Cache-Control max-age or s-maxage, clamped between the policy's Minimum TTL and Maximum TTL; Default TTL (86400s) is used when the origin sends no cache header
Invalidation: aws cloudfront create-invalidation --distribution-id E123 --paths "/index.html" "/img/*"; first 1,000 paths per month are free; it takes minutes and removes the object from every edge
Better than invalidating: versioned filenames (app.v3.js or a content hash) get a new URL, so no invalidation is needed and long TTLs are safe

OAC (Origin Access Control) lets CloudFront sign requests to a private S3 bucket (SigV4) so the bucket stays blocked from public access; it replaces the legacy OAI and supports SSE-KMS and all regions

OAC bucket policy: Principal cloudfront.amazonaws.com, Action s3:GetObject, Condition StringEquals AWS:SourceArn = the distribution ARN; mistake: using the S3 website endpoint, which does not support OAC (it needs a REST endpoint origin)

chapters.title: Route 53 and CloudFront Cheat Sheet
points: Records: A IPv4, AAAA IPv6, CNAME not at apex, Alias free and works at apex for AWS targets
Policies: simple (no health check), weighted (0-255), latency (region based), failover (primary + secondary + health check), geolocation (needs Default)
Health check: 30s interval (10s fast), 3 failures, use a CloudWatch alarm check for private resources
CloudFront: behaviours match in order, Default (*) last, cert in us-east-1, cache key = what you forward
Invalidate: create-invalidation --paths; prefer versioned file names; OAC = principal cloudfront.amazonaws.com plus AWS:SourceArn, REST endpoint only
